claim: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) make up about 40% of the eukaryotic proteome.
source: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) make up about 40% of the eukaryotic proteome (Ward et al., 2004; Holehouse and Kragelund, 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ward et al., 2004 and Holehouse and Kragelund, 2024.

claim: IDPs are characterized by a lack of defined tertiary structure and exist as an ensemble of dynamic, interconverting conformations.
source: Unlike typical well-folded proteins, IDPs are characterized by a lack of defined tertiary structure, and instead exist as an ensemble of dynamic, interconverting conformations (van der Lee et al., 2014; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van der Lee et al., 2014 and Mao et al., 2013.

claim: IDPs play important roles in many biological processes, including regulation of transcription and translation, metabolic signaling, subcellular organization, molecular chaperoning, and response and adaptation to environmental cues.
source: Despite their disordered nature, IDPs are known to play important roles in many biological processes, including regulation of transcription and translation, metabolic signaling, subcellular organization, molecular chaperoning, and response and adaptation to environmental cues (van der Lee et al., 2014; Kedia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van der Lee et al., 2014 and Kedia et al., 2017.

claim: An IDP's sequence determines the ensemble of conformations it adopts, and this ensemble can be important for the IDP's function(s).
source: Different from well-folded proteins, however, an IDP's sequence determines the ensemble of conformations it adopts, and this ensemble can be important for the IDP's function(s) (Holehouse and Kragelund, 2024; Mao et al., 2013; Das et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holehouse and Kragelund, 2024; Mao et al., 2013; and Das et al., 2015.

claim: IDP ensembles have relatively few intramolecular bonds and a large solvent-accessible surface area, which makes their ensembles more sensitive to the physicochemical environment than the relatively rigid structures of well-folded proteins.
source: This is because IDP ensembles have relatively few intramolecular bonds and a large solvent-accessible surface area, which makes their ensembles more sensitive to the physicochemical environment than the relatively rigid structures of well-folded proteins (Moses et al., 2020; Moses et al., 2023; Theillet et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moses et al., 2020; Moses et al., 2023; and Theillet et al., 2014.

claim: Organisms across every biological kingdom can survive near-complete desiccation by entering a state of reversible suspended metabolism known as anhydrobiosis.
source: Organisms across every biological kingdom can survive near-complete desiccation by entering a state of reversible suspended metabolism known as anhydrobiosis (from Greek for 'life without water') (Crowe, 2014; Hesgrove and Boothby, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crowe, 2014 and Hesgrove and Boothby, 2020.

claim: As water effluxes from the cell during drying, the concentration of cosolutes increases by orders of magnitude, dramatically changing the physicochemistry of the cell.
source: As water effluxes from the cell during drying, the concentration of cosolutes increases by orders of magnitude, dramatically changing the physicochemistry of the cell (Romero-Perez et al., 2023; Oliver et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Romero-Perez et al., 2023 and Oliver et al., 2020.

claim: The acquisition of desiccation tolerance has historically been linked to the intracellular buildup of cosolutes such as trehalose, sucrose, arabinose, stachyose, and raffinose in plants and trehalose in some animals, fungi, and bacteria.
source: The acquisition of desiccation tolerance has historically been linked to the intracellular buildup of cosolutes such as trehalose, sucrose, arabinose, stachyose, and raffinose in plants and trehalose in some animals, fungi, and bacteria (Koster and Leopold, 1988; Angeles-Núñez and Tiessen, 2010; Fait et al., 2006; Ryabova et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2022; Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including Koster and Leopold, 1988; Angeles-Núñez and Tiessen, 2010; and others.

claim: The accumulation of high levels of IDPs has been linked to desiccation tolerance in many organisms.
source: More recently, the accumulation of high levels of IDPs has also been linked to desiccation tolerance in many organisms (Hesgrove and Boothby, 2020; Hincha and Thalhammer, 2012; Boothby et al., 2017; Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; Hand et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hesgrove and Boothby, 2020; Hincha and Thalhammer, 2012; and others.

claim: LEA proteins are classified into seven different families based on the presence of conserved motif sequences.
source: LEA proteins are classified into seven different families based on the presence of conserved motif sequences (Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Artur et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008 and Artur et al., 2019.

claim: Trehalose has been shown to enhance IDP protective function in vitro and in vivo.
source: Trehalose, a cosolute enriched alongside IDPs in many desiccation-tolerant systems, has previously been shown to enhance IDP protective function in vitro and in vivo (Nguyen et al., 2022; Goyal et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2018; LeBlanc and Hand, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2022; Goyal et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2018; and LeBlanc and Hand, 2021.

claim: Full-length CAHS D and LEA proteins derived from four different organisms synergize best with endogenous protective cosolutes compared to protective exogenous cosolutes from other organisms.
source: Our result shows that full-length CAHS D and LEA proteins derived from four different organisms synergize better with endogenous protective cosolutes compared to protective exogenous cosolutes from other organisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the LDH protection assays.

claim: The secondary structure (residual helicity) and tertiary structure (radius of gyration) of protective IDPs do not change significantly in the presence of synergistic cosolutes.
source: In all cases, the secondary structure (residual helicity) and tertiary structure (radius of gyration) do not change significantly in the presence of synergistic cosolutes and thus cannot explain the enhancement in function observed with synergistic cosolutes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy and SAXS experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: For CAHS, but not LEA proteins, synergy is related to self-assembly and the formation of a gel.
source: We further demonstrate that for CAHS, but not LEA proteins, synergy is related to self-assembly and the formation of a gel.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC and SAXS experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Functional synergy between IDPs and endogenous cosolutes is a convergent desiccation protection strategy seen among different IDP families and organisms.
source: Our results suggest that functional synergy between IDPs and endogenous cosolutes is a convergent desiccation protection strategy seen among different IDP families and organisms, yet the mechanisms underlying this synergy differ between IDP families.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing synergy across multiple IDP families and organisms.

claim: The mechanisms underlying synergy between IDPs and cosolutes differ between IDP families.
source: Our results suggest that functional synergy between IDPs and endogenous cosolutes is a convergent desiccation protection strategy seen among different IDP families and organisms, yet the mechanisms underlying this synergy differ between IDP families.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing different structural and functional responses to cosolutes for CAHS vs LEA proteins.

claim: Most LEA_4 motifs displayed levels of protection so low that a 50% level of protection could not be reached even at concentrations exceeding 1 mM.
source: Most LEA_4 motifs displayed levels of protection so low that a 50% level of protection could not be reached even at concentrations exceeding 1 mM (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH protection assays shown in Figure 1A, B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Higher concentrations of the LEA_4 motifs tend to inactivate the enzyme when kept under control conditions (4°C) over a 16 hr incubation period during the assay.
source: Additionally, higher concentrations of the LEA_4 motifs tend to inactivate the enzyme when kept under control conditions (4°C, see 'Materials and methods'), over a 16 hr incubation period during the assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The LEA_1 20-mer motif At20 showed robust concentration-dependent protection of LDH.
source: The LEA_1 20-mer motif At20, however, showed robust concentration-dependent protection of LDH, demonstrating that LEA_4 and LEA_1 motifs are functionally distinct (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH protection assays shown in Figure 1A, B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Concentration-dependent protection was observed for trehalose and sucrose.
source: Concentration-dependent protection was also observed for our cosolutes trehalose and sucrose (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH protection assays shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In nearly all cases, synergy was not observed for 11-mer LEA_4 peptides with either sucrose or trehalose.
source: In nearly all cases, synergy was not observed for 11-mer LEA_4 peptides with either sucrose or trehalose. In fact, in several cases, mixing LEA_4 peptides with sucrose or trehalose elicited antagonistic, rather than synergistic, effects (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synergy assays shown in Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The A. thaliana 22- and 44-mer peptides did not synergize with either trehalose or sucrose.
source: Similar to 11-mer motifs, the A. thaliana 22- and 44-mer peptides did not synergize with either trehalose or sucrose (Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synergy assays shown in Figure 1D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The LEA_1 motif At20 is highly protective and synergizes with either sucrose or trehalose.
source: Conversely, the LEA_1 motif tested is highly protective and synergizes with either sucrose or trehalose (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synergy assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: All full-length LEA_1 and LEA_4 proteins confer protection for LDH activity up to the pre-desiccated value.
source: All full-length LEA_1 and LEA_4 proteins confer protection for LDH activity up to the pre-desiccated value (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH protection assays shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CAHS D provided concentration-dependent protection to LDH.
source: Likewise, CAHS D provided concentration-dependent protection to LDH as previously observed (Nguyen et al., 2022; Boothby et al., 2017; Piszkiewicz et al., 2019; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH protection assays shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, as well as citations to previous studies.

claim: Nearly all full-length IDPs showed synergy with either sucrose or trehalose or both.
source: Our results show that nearly all full-length IDPs showed synergy with either sucrose or trehalose or both (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synergy assays shown in Figure 2C, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AvLEA1C, which is derived from a rotifer that accumulates neither trehalose nor sucrose, did not show synergy with either cosolute.
source: Exceptions to this are AvLEA1C, which is derived from a rotifer that accumulates neither trehalose nor sucrose, and BSA, which comes from cows, which of course have no capacity for anhydrobiosis.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from synergy assays and knowledge about the organism's cosolute accumulation.

claim: BSA did not show synergy with either trehalose or sucrose.
source: Exceptions to this are AvLEA1C, which is derived from a rotifer that accumulates neither trehalose nor sucrose, and BSA, which comes from cows, which of course have no capacity for anhydrobiosis.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from synergy assays and knowledge about BSA's source organism.

claim: In cases where LEA proteins displayed synergy, they were always more synergistic with endogenous compared to exogenous cosolutes.
source: Remarkably, in cases where LEA proteins displayed synergy, they were always more synergistic with endogenous compared to exogenous cosolutes (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synergy assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All full-length LEA proteins displayed a single minimum at ~200 nm in CD spectroscopy, indicating that LEA proteins are disordered in the aqueous state.
source: All full-length LEA proteins displayed a single minimum at ~200 nm (Figure 3A, black), indicating that LEA proteins are disordered in the aqueous state.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CAHS D displayed a minimum at ~200 nm and a slight minimum around ~220 nm in CD spectroscopy, indicating that while disordered, it also has some propensity for helical structure in solution.
source: CAHS D also displayed a minimum at ~200 nm and a slight minimum around ~220 nm, indicating that while disordered, it also has some propensity for helical structure in solution (Figure 3A, black), in line with previous studies (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Trehalose and sucrose do not induce any significant structural changes to any of the full-length IDPs tested in the aqueous state.
source: Somewhat to our surprise, trehalose (Figure 3A and C, blue) and sucrose (Figure 3A and C, green) do not induce any significant structural changes to any of the full-length IDPs tested here (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 3A, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All LEA proteins and CAHS D display a significant structural change in the dry state, indicated by a shift from disordered spectra with a minimum at ~200 nm to a helical structure with two minima at ~222 and ~210 nm.
source: Our results show a significant structural change for all LEA proteins and CAHS D in the dry state, indicated by a shift from disordered spectra with a minimum at ~200 nm to a helical structure with two minima at ~222 and ~210 nm (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy of desiccated samples shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BSA showed little change in the CD spectrum upon desiccation.
source: This is in contrast to BSA, which started out helical and showed little change in the spectrum (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy of desiccated samples shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All LEAs and CAHS D display a clear increase in helical propensity upon being desiccated.
source: Using this metric, all LEAs and CAHS D display a clear increase in helical propensity upon being desiccated (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The addition of trehalose or sucrose did not induce significant changes in the secondary structure of LEA and CAHS D proteins in the dry state.
source: As with aqueous samples, the addition of trehalose or sucrose did not induce significant changes in the secondary structure of LEA and CAHS D proteins in the dry state (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CD spectroscopy of desiccated samples shown in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Synergistic protection observed in LDH assays did not correlate with secondary structural changes with the addition of trehalose in aqueous or desiccated states.
source: Synergistic protection observed in our LDH assays did not correlate with secondary structural changes with the addition of trehalose (p=0.973 for aqueous, p=0.2047 for desiccated, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D) or sucrose (p=0.6629 for aqueous, p=0.9763 for desiccated, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: The Rg values obtained for BSA via SAXS match existing literature.
source: The Rg values obtained via this approach match existing literature (Figure 4A; Graewert et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 4A and citation to Graewert et al., 2015.

claim: Adding cosolutes did not modulate the Rg of BSA.
source: Additionally, adding cosolutes did not modulate Rg (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Regardless of the solution environment, all LEA proteins have an Rg that falls within error of readings in other solution environments.
source: We observed that regardless of the solution environment, all of our LEA proteins have an Rg that falls within error of readings in other solution environments (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: At the concentrations used in SAXS experiments, cosolutes do not induce significant changes in the global dimensions of LEA proteins.
source: At the concentrations used here, cosolutes do not induce significant changes in the global dimensions of LEA proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from SAXS experiments.

claim: The 160:1 trehalose solution with CAHS D had a Guinier region that was sharply curved upward, consistent with the presence of large oligomerized species.
source: While this Rg was consistent in 1.6:1 disaccharide solutions, 16:1 disaccharide solutions, and 160:1 sucrose solution, we found that the 160:1 trehalose solution had a Guinier region that was sharply curved upward, even upon the protein's first exposure to the X-ray source (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G). This is consistent with the presence of large oligomerized species.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The 160:1 trehalose sample with CAHS D had a predicted molecular weight about 1000% higher than other samples.
source: In contrast, the 160:1 sucrose sample had a pMW about 300% higher than other samples, and the 160:1 trehalose sample had a pMW about 1000% higher (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 4G.

claim: All LEA proteins showed a propensity to form oligomers, even at low concentrations.
source: All of our LEA proteins showed a propensity to form oligomers, even at low concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PICUP shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of trehalose or sucrose did not elicit changes in oligomeric populations of LEA proteins.
source: However, the presence of trehalose or sucrose did not elicit changes in oligomeric populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PICUP shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 0.235 mM, CAHS D does not undergo a characteristic gel melt indicating a lack of gelation.
source: Consistent with this, at 0.235 mM, we find that CAHS D does not undergo a characteristic gel melt indicating a lack of gelation (Figure 5A, black).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of trehalose and sucrose at increasing molar ratios (1:1, 10:1, 100:1, and 500:1) to CAHS D at 0.235 mM showed thermal features characteristic of endothermic phase transitions, indicating that the presence of these cosolutes induced gelation.
source: Addition of trehalose and sucrose at increasing molar ratios (1:1, 10:1, 100:1, and 500:1) showed thermal features characteristic of endothermic phase transitions (e.g., a gel melting), indicating that the presence of these cosolutes induced gelation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Trehalose induced significant gelation of CAHS D at a 100:1 ratio, while 500:1 of sucrose was required to induce a significant gel melt.
source: Trehalose induced significant gelation at a 100:1 ratio, while 500:1 of sucrose was required to induce a significant gel melt (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Trehalose has a larger influence than sucrose on the gelation of CAHS D.
source: This is consistent with trehalose producing larger oligomeric species in our SAXS experiments (Figure 4G), indicating that trehalose has a larger influence than sucrose on the gelation of CAHS D (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data from DSC and SAXS shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4G.

claim: Addition of trehalose or sucrose at increasing molar concentrations promoted the formation of stronger gels of CAHS D at 12 mg/mL.
source: Addition of trehalose or sucrose at increasing molar concentrations promoted the formation of stronger gels evident by the enthalpy of melting measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: None of the LEA proteins tested by themselves or in mixtures with trehalose or sucrose show evidence of gelation.
source: None of our LEA proteins by themselves or in mixtures with trehalose or sucrose show evidence of gelation (Figure 5B–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5B-G.

claim: BSA failed to form a gel.
source: Likewise, BSA also failed to form a gel (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Unlike trehalose and sucrose, below the protein's gelation threshold no increase in enthalpy of melting was observed upon the addition of glycine betaine to CAHS D.
source: Unlike trehalose and sucrose, below the protein's gelation threshold no increase in enthalpy of melting was observed upon the addition of glycine betaine (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: A decrease in enthalpy of melting was observed when glycine betaine was present at the 500:1 molar ratio with CAHS D above the protein's gelation threshold, signifying inhibition of CAHS D gelation.
source: While trehalose and sucrose enhanced gelation of CAHS D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E), we observed a decrease in enthalpy of melting when glycine betaine was present at the 500:1 molar ratio, signifying inhibition of CAHS D gelation (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DSC shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: A non-gelling concentration of CAHS D in 1000:1 glycine betaine yielded a scattering profile similar to the protein with no cosolute indicating a lack of gelation.
source: A non-gelling concentration of CAHS D in 1000:1 glycine betaine yielded a scattering profile similar to the protein with no cosolute indicating a lack of gelation (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 1000:1 sucrose and trehalose with CAHS D yielded scattering profiles consistent with gelation.
source: Meanwhile, 1000:1 sucrose and trehalose yielded scattering profiles consistent with gelation, similar to those previously reported (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SAXS shown in Figure 6G and citation to Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023.

claim: Glycine betaine on its own is not protective to LDH during drying nor does it inhibit LDH activity.
source: Glycine betaine on its own is not protective to LDH during drying nor does it inhibit LDH activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A significant antagonistic relationship was found between glycine betaine and CAHS D on LDH protection.
source: We found a significant antagonistic relationship between glycine betaine and CAHS D on LDH protection (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LDH synergy assays shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Endogenous cosolutes enriched during desiccation enhance the protective capacity of CAHS D, full-length LEA_4, and LEA_1 proteins in an in vitro enzyme assay.
source: For the proteins we tested empirically, we demonstrate that endogenous cosolutes enriched during desiccation enhance the protective capacity of CAHS D, full-length LEA_4, and LEA_1 proteins in an in vitro enzyme assay.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from LDH protection and synergy assays.

claim: Synergistic cosolutes induced oligomerization and gelation of CAHS D.
source: However, synergistic cosolutes did induce oligomerization and gelation of CAHS D.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from SAXS and DSC experiments.

claim: In the case of CAHS D, but not LEAs, oligomerization, gelation, and protective synergy can be traced to direct interactions between cosolute and protective protein.
source: Finally, we show that in the case of CAHS D, but not LEAs, oligomerization, gelation, and protective synergy can be traced to direct interactions between cosolute and protective protein.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from multiple assays and computational analysis using transfer free energies.

claim: Functional synergy for the full-length proteins from different organisms mirrored the endogenous cosolute environment in that organism.
source: Functional synergy for the full-length proteins from different organisms mirrored the endogenous cosolute environment in that organism. In all cases, an IDP protected LDH activity more with its endogenous cosolute compared to an exogenous cosolute.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from LDH synergy assays.

claim: Both tardigrade proteins used in this study synergized with trehalose at an order of magnitude lower concentration than what was required to elicit synergy with the nematode LEA protein.
source: For example, nematodes and tardigrades both accumulate trehalose during desiccation, but tardigrades accumulate orders of magnitude less (Nguyen et al., 2022; Higa and Womersley, 1993; Browne et al., 2004; Hengherr et al., 2008). Consistent with this, both tardigrade proteins used in this study synergized with trehalose at an order of magnitude lower concentration than what was required to elicit synergy with the nematode LEA protein.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from LDH synergy assays and citations to studies on cosolute accumulation.

claim: LEA proteins are known to stabilize sugar glasses in a dry state.
source: In line with this, recent studies have highlighted the ability of LEA proteins to stabilize sugar glasses in a dry state (Shimizu et al., 2010; Wolkers et al., 2001; Shih et al., 2012; Hincha et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shimizu et al., 2010; Wolkers et al., 2001; Shih et al., 2012; and Hincha et al., 2021.

claim: Glass formation is known to preserve labile biomolecules during desiccation, contributing to survival.
source: Glass formation is known to preserve labile biomolecules during desiccation, contributing to survival (Boothby et al., 2017; Sakurai et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boothby et al., 2017 and Sakurai et al., 2008.

claim: There are known links between type II diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.
source: For example, there are known links between type II diabetes and Alzheimer's disease, and it has been shown that the intrinsically disordered neurodegenerative peptide Aβ42 undergoes pathological oligomerization in the presence of glucose whose levels mirror those found in diabetic patients (Kedia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kedia et al., 2017.

claim: The intrinsically disordered neurodegenerative peptide Aβ42 undergoes pathological oligomerization in the presence of glucose whose levels mirror those found in diabetic patients.
source: For example, there are known links between type II diabetes and Alzheimer's disease, and it has been shown that the intrinsically disordered neurodegenerative peptide Aβ42 undergoes pathological oligomerization in the presence of glucose whose levels mirror those found in diabetic patients (Kedia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kedia et al., 2017.

claim: LEA_4 motifs have previously been suggested to be sufficient to confer desiccation protection to desiccation-sensitive proteins and membranes to a degree similar to full-length LEA proteins, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Interestingly, LEA_4 motifs have previously been suggested to be sufficient to confer desiccation protection to desiccation-sensitive proteins and membranes to a degree similar to full-length LEA proteins, both in vitro and in vivo (Furuki and Sakurai, 2016; Furuki et al., 2012; Furuki and Sakurai, 2014; Hibshman and Goldstein, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Furuki and Sakurai, 2016; Furuki et al., 2012; Furuki and Sakurai, 2014; and Hibshman and Goldstein, 2021.

claim: Family 1 LEA (LEA_1) proteins are characterized by a 20-mer repeating motif.
source: Family 1 LEA (LEA_1) proteins are characterized by a 20-mer repeating motif, whereas Family 4 LEA (LEA_4) proteins are characterized by the repetition of an 11-mer LEA_4 motif (Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; Dure L 3rd, 1993; Knox-Brown et al., 2020; Furuki and Sakurai, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; and others.

claim: Family 4 LEA (LEA_4) proteins are characterized by the repetition of an 11-mer LEA_4 motif.
source: Family 1 LEA (LEA_1) proteins are characterized by a 20-mer repeating motif, whereas Family 4 LEA (LEA_4) proteins are characterized by the repetition of an 11-mer LEA_4 motif (Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; Dure L 3rd, 1993; Knox-Brown et al., 2020; Furuki and Sakurai, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; and others.

claim: LEA motifs are often found in multiple linear or nonlinear repeats across the length of a LEA protein.
source: These motifs are often found in multiple linear or nonlinear repeats across the length of a LEA protein (Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; Dure L 3rd, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hundertmark and Hincha, 2008; Battaglia et al., 2008; and Dure L 3rd, 1993.

claim: LEA proteins gain helical conformation upon drying or in response to low water availability.
source: LEA proteins gain helical conformation upon drying or in response to low water availability. Drying-induced helicity has been postulated to drive their protective function (Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; LeBlanc and Hand, 2021; Cuevas-Velazquez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; LeBlanc and Hand, 2021; and Cuevas-Velazquez et al., 2016.

claim: Drying-induced helicity of LEA proteins has been postulated to drive their protective function.
source: LEA proteins gain helical conformation upon drying or in response to low water availability. Drying-induced helicity has been postulated to drive their protective function (Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; LeBlanc and Hand, 2021; Cuevas-Velazquez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; LeBlanc and Hand, 2021; and Cuevas-Velazquez et al., 2016.

claim: CAHS D oligomers, as well as those of other CAHS proteins, have been reported to undergo self-assembly to form a gel network.
source: CAHS D oligomers, as well as those of other CAHS proteins, have been reported to undergo self-assembly to form a gel network (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Eicher et al., 2022; Malki et al., 2022; Yagi-Utsumi et al., 2021; Tanaka et al., 2022; Eicher et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Eicher et al., 2022; and others.

claim: Both CAHS and LEA proteins are known to oligomerize.
source: We next assessed quaternary structure as both CAHS and LEA proteins are known to oligomerize (Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023), and for CAHS proteins, oligomerization leads to gelation (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Eicher et al., 2022; Malki et al., 2022; Yagi-Utsumi et al., 2021; Tanaka et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022 and Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023.

claim: For CAHS proteins, oligomerization leads to gelation.
source: We next assessed quaternary structure as both CAHS and LEA proteins are known to oligomerize (Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023), and for CAHS proteins, oligomerization leads to gelation (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Eicher et al., 2022; Malki et al., 2022; Yagi-Utsumi et al., 2021; Tanaka et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies including Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023; Eicher et al., 2022; and others.

claim: LEA oligomerization appears to be weak and transient, requiring extreme crowding and/or sensitive methods to detect.
source: However, LEA oligomerization appears to be weak and transient, requiring extreme crowding and/or sensitive methods to detect (Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; Shou et al., 2019; Rivera-Najera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hernández-Sánchez et al., 2022; Shou et al., 2019; and Rivera-Najera et al., 2014.

claim: PICUP has previously been used to characterize oligomeric forms in LEA proteins in vitro.
source: PICUP has previously been used to characterize oligomeric forms in LEA proteins in vitro (Rivera-Najera et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rivera-Najera et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: CAHS D dimer formation is a necessary step toward gelation.
source: We reasoned that dimerization is indicative of gelation since CAHS D dimers were especially prevalent in crosslinking data (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023), and previous research suggests that CAHS D dimer formation is a necessary step toward gelation (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana accumulates both sucrose and trehalose at high levels during desiccation.
source: These organisms include the plant Arabidopsis thaliana (AtLEA3-3), the nematode Aphelenchus avenae (AavLEA1), the tardigrade Hypsibius exemplaris (HeLEA68614), and the rotifer Adineta vaga (AvLEA1C) (Table 1). To assess whether synergy extends across LEA families, we selected a LEA_1 protein from A. thaliana (AtLEA4-2) (Table 1). Finally, CAHS D was selected from the tardigrade H. exemplaris (Table 1). These organisms were selected not only because they all utilize LEA proteins to survive desiccation, but also because they accumulate different disaccharides to varying degrees during drying (Angeles-Núñez and Tiessen, 2010; Fait et al., 2006; Nguyen et al., 2022; Higa and Womersley, 1993; Browne et al., 2004; Hengherr et al., 2008; Tunnacliffe and Lapinski, 2003; Lapinski and Tunnacliffe, 2003; Table 1).

claim: LDH retains only approximately 2% of its pre-desiccation activity when dried and rehydrated without protectants.
source: LDH assay is used to assess the function of desiccation protectants to protect the activity of LDH, which otherwise retains only approximately 2% of its pre-desiccation activity when dried and rehydrated (Nguyen et al., 2022; Boothby et al., 2017; Goyal et al., 2005; Piszkiewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2022; Boothby et al., 2017; Goyal et al., 2005; and Piszkiewicz et al., 2019.

claim: The radius of gyration calculated for CAHS D in this study is approximately 5 angstroms greater than previously reported.
source: We note that the radius of gyration that we calculated for CAHS D is approximately 5 angstroms greater than previously reported by our group (Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data from this study with previous work cited as Sanchez-Martinez et al., 2023.

claim: The difference in CAHS D radius of gyration can be attributed to minor differences in the experimental approach, specifically the omission of the SEC step in this study.
source: We believe that this difference can be attributed to minor differences in our approach. While we used size-exclusion chromatography (SEC)-coupled SAXS and a relatively dilute CAHS D sample in our previous study, the number of SAXS experiments in this study necessitated a higher-throughput approach that omitted the SEC step.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from methodological differences between studies.

claim: Control samples of CAHS D in this study contained a higher fraction of transient oligomeric species, which inflated the radius of gyration without significantly curving the Guinier region.
source: We therefore believe that our control samples contained a higher fraction of transient oligomeric species, which inflated the radius of gyration without significantly curving the Guinier region.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Trehalose and sucrose both form glasses when dried.
source: Because trehalose and sucrose both form glasses when dried (Crowe et al., 1998; Simperler et al., 2006), it is possible that our LEA proteins are inducing a change in the glass's structural properties that leads to synergy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crowe et al., 1998 and Simperler et al., 2006.

claim: Repulsive cosolutes can promote heterotypic interactions between LEAs and other proteins.
source: While repulsive cosolutes drive homotypic interactions between CAHS D monomers, the same thermodynamic force can promote heterotypic interactions between LEAs and other proteins (Riback et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Riback et al., 2020.

claim: Sucrose may act as a crowder eliciting an excluded volume effect on CAHS D.
source: While sucrose does not drive dimerization through direct 'soft' repulsion, it may still do so by acting as a crowder eliciting an excluded volume effect (Sarkar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation to Sarkar et al., 2013.

claim: The use of a single cosolute-IDP system in the in vitro experiments does not accurately mirror the diverse cosolute changes in desiccating systems.
source: It is important to note that desiccation-tolerant organisms employ multiple cosolutes to counteract the effects of desiccation. The use of a single cosolute-IDP system in our in vitro experiments does not accurately mirror the diverse cosolute changes in desiccating systems.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of biological systems and inference about experimental limitations.

claim: Desiccation-tolerant organisms employ multiple cosolutes to counteract the effects of desiccation.
